questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fever, myalgia, and headache. She worked on a farm near Savannah, Georgia. Though she did not recall any recent rashes or illness, she removed at least two ticks from her skin in the past month. She had a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. She was taking losartan, metformin, and gliclazide. On examination, the patient appeared ill. Her temperature was 39.3°C (102.7°F); other vital signs were normal. Examination was otherwise unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 2.3 ×109/L Platelet count 92 ×109/L ALT 84 U/L Peripheral blood smear:
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Ehrlichia chaffeensis HME, or ehrlichiosis, is caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, an intracellular pathogen that infects monocytes. The image shows morulae within monocytes. This is diagnostic for HME.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q31

questions.question: You are asked to see a woman in her 40's who lives in Montreal and who has never traveled. She presented with fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, and migratory arthralgias. She also developed a maculopapular rash on her extremities that became petechial and purpuric. She was seen in the ER 5 days ago. See picture of her rash and Gram stain of her blood culture.

parts.text: What ONE epidemiological question do you ask her?
What is the organism? Name to species level.
If this was suspected on initial presentation, why should the microbiology lab be notified?

questions.model_answer: a) Key epidemiologic question: any recent travel history is stated as none, so ask about tick exposure (outdoor/wooded activity, camping, pets) or contact with a laboratory/research setting handling Rickettsia, since RMSF can rarely occur without travel via local tick exposure or lab-acquired infection; specifically ask about recent tick bite/outdoor exposure. b) Organism (to species): Rickettsia rickettsii. c) Notify the lab because: R. rickettsii is a biosafety risk to laboratory personnel (highly infectious via aerosol/inoculation), requiring BSL-3 handling precautions; advance notice prevents routine processing that could expose lab staff. d) Treatment: doxycycline (drug of choice regardless of age, including pregnancy in severe/life-threatening disease), started empirically without waiting for confirmatory testing given high mortality if treatment delayed.

questions.question: Otherwise healthy 17 M with painful and pruritic rash on hands and feet, well demarcated at wrists and ankles

parts.text: One simple investigation to confirm dx?

cohort_answer.text: Papular-purpuric gloves and socks syndrome (PPGSS) - 2/3 assoc with parvovirus B19, sporadically VZV/EBV/CMV/HSV6-7/Coxsackie/HepB/Rubella; self-resolving 7-14 days. Investigation: IgM parvovirus B19 (positive up to 2-3 months post-infection), can also check IgG avidity

questions.question: A woman travels to Tanzania and climbs Mount Kilimanjaro. She presents with a fever and eschar.

cohort_answer.text: African trypanosomiasis; Tularemia; Rickettsia africae (African tick bite fever); Scrub typhus; Bacillus anthracis; Plague.

questions.question: [image-based question: picture of a tick, looked like Dermacentor]

parts.text: Name 1 infection associated with this tick.

questions.model_answer: Dermacentor tick (dog tick/wood tick) - associated with Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii); also transmits tularemia (Francisella tularensis) and Colorado tick fever.
